    Pell Equations

    Introduction

    This article discusses the solution of the (generalized) Pell equation. The generalized Pell equation is the Diophantine equation in 𝑥x and 𝑦y

    𝑥2−𝐷𝑦2=𝑁,x2−Dy2=N,

    where 𝐷D is a positive integer that is not a perfect square[^not-square], and 𝑁N is a nonzero integer. The Pell equation in the narrow sense refers specifically to the special cases 𝑁 =1N=1 or 𝑁 = ±1N=±1, and sometimes also includes the case 𝑁 = ±4N=±4. The generalized Pell equation is closely related to finding quadratic integers with norm 𝑁N in the real quadratic integer ring, and these cases often referred to as the (narrow sense) Pell equation can be viewed as finding units in the real quadratic integer ring.

    When this article mentions Pell's equation, it specifically refers to the case 𝑁 =1N=1. Accordingly, the case 𝑁 = −1N=−1 is called the negative Pell equation[^neg-pell].

    Structure of Solutions

    The integer solutions (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) of the generalized Pell equation are closely related to the quadratic integers 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD. For this reason, solutions of Pell's equation in the literature are often written in the form 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD. Since the norm of a quadratic integer is

    𝑁(𝑥+𝑦√𝐷)=𝑥2−𝐷𝑦2,N(x+yD)=x2−Dy2,

    the generalized Pell equation is roughly equivalent to finding quadratic integers with norm 𝑁N. However, there is a subtle difference between them. When both 𝑥x and 𝑦y are integers, 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD is certainly a quadratic integer; conversely, a quadratic integer does not necessarily require both 𝑥x and 𝑦y to be integers—in the case 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4), 𝑥x and 𝑦y can also both be half-integers[^half-int].

    This distinction is particularly important when finding fundamental units. Since a unit in the quadratic integer ring is a quadratic integer with norm ±1±1. For 𝐷 ≡2,3(mod4)D≡2,3(mod4), to find such a unit, one only needs to solve the generalized Pell equation with 𝑁 = ±1N=±1; but for 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4), the case 𝑁 = ±4N=±4 also needs to be considered. The solution method for units will be discussed below.

    To understand the structure of solutions to the generalized Pell equation, one must start with the Brahmagupta identity:

    (𝑥21−𝐷𝑦21)(𝑥22−𝐷𝑦22)=(𝑥1𝑥2+𝐷𝑦1𝑦2)2−𝐷(𝑥1𝑦2+𝑥2𝑦1)2.(x12−Dy12)(x22−Dy22)=(x1x2+Dy1y2)2−D(x1y2+x2y1)2.

    This is equivalent to the norm of quadratic integers being multiplicative, i.e.,

    𝑁(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷)𝑁(𝑥2+𝑦2√𝐷)=𝑁((𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷)(𝑥2+𝑦2√𝐷))=𝑁((𝑥1𝑥2+𝐷𝑦1𝑦2)+(𝑥1𝑦2+𝑥2𝑦1)√𝐷).N(x1+y1D)N(x2+y2D)=N((x1+y1D)(x2+y2D))=N((x1x2+Dy1y2)+(x1y2+x2y1)D).

    Using this identity, one can combine integer solutions of 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁1x2−Dy2=N1 and 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁2x2−Dy2=N2 to obtain integer solutions of 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁1𝑁2x2−Dy2=N1N2. Of course, from the perspective of quadratic integers, combining solutions is just multiplying quadratic integers, which demonstrates the convenience of representing Pell equation solutions as quadratic integers. In particular, taking 𝑁1 =𝑁N1=N and 𝑁2 =1N2=1, if one knows a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N and all solutions to the corresponding Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1, then more solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N can be obtained. Of course, this method may not generate all solutions. However, this at least shows that understanding the solution structure of the Pell equation is important for understanding the solution structure of the generalized Pell equation.

    Pell's Equation

    The geometric meaning of the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1 is a hyperbola with the real axis as the 𝑥x-axis and the imaginary axis as the 𝑦y-axis. Each point on the hyperbola uniquely corresponds to a nonzero value of 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD: the left branch of the hyperbola corresponds to negative values of 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD, while the right branch corresponds to positive values. Moreover, on each branch, as one moves from bottom to top, the values of 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD are strictly increasing. The values of quadratic integers give the solutions of Pell's equation a natural ordering.

    The hyperbola is symmetric about both the 𝑥x-axis and 𝑦y-axis, so to discuss solutions of Pell's equation one only needs to consider the segment in the first quadrant; the remaining solutions can be obtained through symmetry. This is equivalent to considering only solutions with 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷 >1x+yD>1. If the equation has nontrivial solutions beyond ( ±1,0)(±1,0), there must exist a solution (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) in the first quadrant with the smallest value of 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD, which is also the integer point with the smallest horizontal and vertical coordinates in the first quadrant (excluding the axes). This is called the fundamental solution of Pell's equation[^fundamental-solution]. According to the previous discussion, integer pairs (𝑥𝑘,𝑦𝑘)(xk,yk) satisfying 𝑥𝑘 +𝑦𝑘√𝐷 =(𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷)𝑘xk+ykD=(x1+y1D)k are all solutions of Pell's equation and lie in the first quadrant. Conversely, these are indeed all solutions of Pell's equation in the first quadrant. Using symmetry again, we obtain the following conclusion:

    Theorem

    Let (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) be the fundamental solution of the Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1. Then all its solutions are

    {(𝑥,𝑦):𝑥+𝑦√𝐷=±(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷)𝑘,𝑘∈𝐙}.{(x,y):x+yD=±(x1+y1D)k,k∈Z}.
    Proof

    First, prove that there are no other solutions in the first quadrant. Suppose there is another solution 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD and for some 𝑘 ≥0k≥0,

    𝑥𝑘+𝑦𝑘√𝐷<𝑥+𝑦√𝐷<𝑥𝑘+1+𝑦𝑘+1√𝐷.xk+ykD<x+yD<xk+1+yk+1D.

    Geometrically, this means the integer point (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) lies between the points (𝑥𝑘,𝑦𝑘)(xk,yk) and (𝑥𝑘+1,𝑦𝑘+1)(xk+1,yk+1) on the hyperbola (excluding the endpoints). Multiplying the inequality by 𝑥𝑘 −𝑦𝑘√𝐷 =(𝑥𝑘 +𝑦𝑘√𝐷)−1xk−ykD=(xk+ykD)−1 gives

    1<(𝑥+𝑦√𝐷)(𝑥𝑘−𝑦𝑘√𝐷)=(𝑥𝑥𝑘−𝐷𝑦𝑦𝑘)+(𝑥𝑘𝑦−𝑥𝑦𝑘)√𝐷<𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷.1<(x+yD)(xk−ykD)=(xxk−Dyyk)+(xky−xyk)D<x1+y1D.

    According to the monotonicity mentioned earlier, this inequality shows that (𝑥𝑥𝑘 −𝐷𝑦𝑦𝑘,𝑥𝑘𝑦 −𝑥𝑦𝑘)(xxk−Dyyk,xky−xyk) is an integer point between (1,0)(1,0) and (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1). This contradicts the choice of (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1).

    When extending solutions from the first quadrant to the entire plane, taking the reciprocal (negating the exponent 𝑘k) corresponds to symmetry about the 𝑥x-axis, and taking the overall negative corresponds to symmetry about the origin. Together with the trivial solution when 𝑘 =0k=0, we obtain all solutions of Pell's equation.

    The previous discussion only assumed the existence of a fundamental solution. Now we need to show that Pell's equation always has nontrivial solutions.

    Theorem

    The Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1 always has integer solutions other than ( ±1,0)(±1,0).

    Proof

    First, Dirichlet's Theorem shows that there exist infinitely many pairs of positive integers (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) such that

    ∣𝑥𝑦−√𝐷∣≤1𝑦2|xy−D|≤1y2

    holds. They all satisfy

    |𝑥2−𝐷𝑦2|=𝑦2∣𝑥𝑦−√𝐷∣∣𝑥𝑦+√𝐷∣≤1𝑦2+2√𝐷<1+2√𝐷.|x2−Dy2|=y2|xy−D||xy+D|≤1y2+2D<1+2D.

    Therefore, there must exist an integer 𝑚 ∈( −1 −2√𝐷,1 +2√𝐷)m∈(−1−2D,1+2D) such that there are infinitely many pairs (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) satisfying 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑚x2−Dy2=m. Grouping these (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) by their remainders modulo 𝑚m, we know that for some pair of integers (𝑥0,𝑦0)(x0,y0), there are infinitely many (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) such that 𝑥 ≡𝑥0(mod𝑚)x≡x0(modm) and 𝑦 ≡𝑦0(mod𝑚)y≡y0(modm) hold. Taking any two distinct pairs (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) and (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) satisfying these conditions, then

    𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷𝑥2+𝑦2√𝐷=𝑥1𝑥2−𝐷𝑦1𝑦2𝑚+𝑥2𝑦1−𝑥1𝑦2𝑚√𝐷.x1+y1Dx2+y2D=x1x2−Dy1y2m+x2y1−x1y2mD.

    Because according to the congruence relations,

    𝑥1𝑥2−𝐷𝑦1𝑦2≡𝑥20−𝐷𝑦20=𝑚≡0(mod|𝑚|),𝑥2𝑦1−𝑥1𝑦2≡𝑥0𝑦0−𝑥0𝑦0=0(mod|𝑚|),x1x2−Dy1y2≡x02−Dy02=m≡0(mod|m|),x2y1−x1y2≡x0y0−x0y0=0(mod|m|),

    this shows the right-hand side yields integer solutions. Moreover, since (𝑥1,𝑦1) ≠(𝑥2,𝑦2)(x1,y1)≠(x2,y2), it is nontrivial. This demonstrates that Pell's equation indeed has nontrivial solutions.

    Of course, this section provides a non-constructive proof. When discussing solution methods for Pell's equation below, we will directly use the convergent of continued fractions to construct solutions to Pell's equation, thus providing another proof of the existence of nontrivial solutions to Pell's equation. Additionally, although the solution structure of Pell's equation obtained in this section is consistent with the structure of units in the real quadratic integer ring, for the case 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4), this section does not completely resolve the structure problem of units in the corresponding quadratic integer ring, which will be discussed further below.

    Generalized Pell Equation

    The graph of the generalized Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N is also a hyperbola in the plane, also symmetric about the 𝑥x-axis and 𝑦y-axis. As noted earlier, some solutions of the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N may differ by a factor that is a solution of the Pell equation, which means the solutions of 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N can be divided into equivalence classes. For two solutions (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) and (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) of 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N, if there exists a solution (𝑢,𝑣)(u,v) of the Pell equation such that 𝑥2 +𝑦2√𝐷 =(𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷)(𝑢 +𝑣√𝐷)x2+y2D=(x1+y1D)(u+vD), then the solutions (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) and (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) are said to be equivalent. The necessary and sufficient condition for two solutions to be equivalent is

    𝑁∣(𝑥1𝑥2−𝐷𝑦1𝑦2), 𝑁∣(𝑥2𝑦1−𝑥1𝑦2).N∣(x1x2−Dy1y2), N∣(x2y1−x1y2).

    Since solutions of the Pell equation are relatively easy to find, a natural idea is to find one solution in each of the above equivalence classes. Once these solutions are known, all solutions of the generalized Pell equation can be obtained using the corresponding solutions of the Pell equation. In the equivalence classes of solutions to the generalized Pell equation, due to symmetry, each equivalence class has a solution with non-negative 𝑦y that is as small as possible: if such a solution is unique, it is called the fundamental solution of that equivalence class; otherwise, the equivalence class must have two solutions with non-negative 𝑦y that are minimal, and they are symmetric about the 𝑦y-axis, in which case we choose the one with 𝑥 >0x>0 as the fundamental solution. Thus, solving the generalized Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N is equivalent to solving for its fundamental solution set 𝑈U. Let the fundamental solution of the corresponding Pell equation be (𝑟,𝑠)(r,s), then the set of all solutions of the generalized Pell equation is

    {(𝑥,𝑦):𝑥+𝑦√𝐷=±(𝑟+𝑠√𝐷)𝑘(𝑢+𝑣√𝐷),𝑘∈𝐙,𝑢+𝑣√𝐷∈𝑈}.{(x,y):x+yD=±(r+sD)k(u+vD),k∈Z,u+vD∈U}.

    The fundamental solutions of the generalized Pell equation are necessarily finite. This is because from the general solution expression above, the absolute value |𝑢 +𝑣√𝐷||u+vD| must lie between 𝑟 −𝑠√𝐷r−sD and 𝑟 +𝑠√𝐷r+sD. References at the end of the article provide stricter estimates for the range of coordinates of fundamental solutions. Of course, unlike the case of Pell's equation, the generalized Pell equation may have no solutions.

    In addition to combining solutions, the method of obtaining all solutions in the same equivalence class using a solution (𝑢,𝑣)(u,v) of the generalized Pell equation and the fundamental solution (𝑟,𝑠)(r,s) of the Pell equation can also use the following recurrence relation

    𝑥𝑘=2𝑟𝑥𝑘−1−𝑥𝑘−2, 𝑦𝑘=2𝑟𝑦𝑘−1−𝑦𝑘−2,xk=2rxk−1−xk−2, yk=2ryk−1−yk−2,

    where 𝑥𝑘 +𝑦𝑘√𝐷 =(𝑟 +𝑠√𝐷)𝑘(𝑢 +𝑣√𝐷)xk+ykD=(r+sD)k(u+vD). This is because both 𝑥𝑘xk and 𝑦𝑘yk can be written in the form 𝐴(𝑟 +𝑠√𝐷)𝑘 +𝐵(𝑟 −𝑠√𝐷)𝑘A(r+sD)k+B(r−sD)k for some pair of real numbers (𝐴,𝐵)(A,B), and according to Vieta's theorem, 𝑟 ±𝑠√𝐷r±sD are the two real roots of the equation 𝑥2 −2𝑟𝑥 +1 =0x2−2rx+1=0, so 𝑥𝑛xn and 𝑦𝑛yn both satisfy the above second-order linear recurrence relation with constant coefficients. Compared to combining solutions, this recurrence formula has fewer multiplications.

    Solution Methods

    The solutions of both Pell's equation and the generalized Pell equation can be obtained based on continued fractions.

    PQa Algorithm

    The algorithms discussed in this article are all based on the PQa algorithm, which can be used to find the continued fraction expansion of a specific quadratic irrational.

    Let integers 𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷P0,Q0,D satisfy 𝑄0 ≠0Q0≠0, 𝐷 >0D>0 and not a perfect square, and 𝑃20 ≡𝐷(mod𝑄0)P02≡D(modQ0). Then the continued fraction expansion [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯][a0,a1,⋯] of the quadratic irrational

    𝜔=𝑃0+√𝐷𝑄0ω=P0+DQ0

    can be obtained through the following recurrence formula:

    𝑎𝑘=⌊𝑃𝑘+√𝐷𝑄𝑘⌋, 𝑃𝑘+1=𝑎𝑘𝑄𝑘−𝑃𝑘, 𝑄𝑘+1=𝐷−𝑃2𝑘+1𝑄𝑘.ak=⌊Pk+DQk⌋, Pk+1=akQk−Pk, Qk+1=D−Pk+12Qk.

    Furthermore, the numerator and denominator 𝐴𝑘Ak and 𝐵𝑘Bk of the 𝑘k-th convergent of 𝜔ω are given by the following recurrence formula:

    𝐴𝑘=𝑎𝑘𝐴𝑘−1+𝐴𝑘−2, 𝐵𝑘=𝑎𝑘𝐵𝑘−1+𝐵𝑘−2Ak=akAk−1+Ak−2, Bk=akBk−1+Bk−2

    with 𝐴−1 =1A−1=1, 𝐴−2 =0A−2=0, 𝐵−1 =0B−1=0, 𝐵−2 =1B−2=1.

    The correctness of these formulas has been proven in the article on continued fractions. There it is also explained that because quadratic irrationals are periodic continued fractions, the triple (𝑃𝑘,𝑄𝑘,𝑎𝑘)(Pk,Qk,ak) will eventually enter a cycle, so the algorithm always terminates in a finite number of steps. Let the minimal period length be ℓℓ, and the earliest starting position of the cycle be 𝑘0k0, then the continued fraction expansion of the quadratic irrational can be written as

    𝜔=[𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘0−1,―――――――𝑎𝑘0,⋯,𝑎𝑘0+ℓ−1].ω=[a0,⋯,ak0−1,ak0,⋯,ak0+ℓ−1―].

    To solve Pell's equation using the PQa algorithm, the following theorem is needed:

    Theorem

    Continuing with the above notation. Let 𝐺𝑘 =𝑄0𝐴𝑘 −𝑃0𝐵𝑘Gk=Q0Ak−P0Bk, then the integer pair (𝐺𝑘−1,𝐵𝑘−1)(Gk−1,Bk−1) satisfies

    𝐺2𝑘−1−𝐷𝐵2𝑘−1=(−1)𝑘𝑄0𝑄𝑘,Gk−12−DBk−12=(−1)kQ0Qk,

    and their greatest common divisor gcd(𝐺𝑘−1,𝐵𝑘−1)gcd(Gk−1,Bk−1) divides 𝑄𝑘Qk.

    Proof

    Let the 𝑘k-th remainder (complete quotient) in the continued fraction expansion of 𝜔ω be 𝜔𝑘ωk, that is,

    𝜔=[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘−1,𝜔𝑘]=𝜔𝑘𝐴𝑘−1+𝐴𝑘−2𝜔𝑘𝐵𝑘−1+𝐵𝑘−2.ω=[a0,a1,⋯,ak−1,ωk]=ωkAk−1+Ak−2ωkBk−1+Bk−2.

    Substituting 𝜔 =(𝑃0 +√𝐷)/𝑄0ω=(P0+D)/Q0 and 𝜔𝑘 =(𝑃𝑘 +√𝐷)/𝑄𝑘ωk=(Pk+D)/Qk into the above gives

    𝑃0+√𝐷𝑄0=(𝑃𝑘+√𝐷)𝐴𝑘−1+𝑄𝑘𝐴𝑘−2(𝑃𝑘+√𝐷)𝐵𝑘−1+𝑄𝑘𝐵𝑘−2.P0+DQ0=(Pk+D)Ak−1+QkAk−2(Pk+D)Bk−1+QkBk−2.

    After eliminating denominators on both sides and comparing coefficients of rational and irrational parts, then substituting the expression for 𝐺𝑘Gk, we obtain:

    𝐺𝑘−1=𝑃𝑘𝐵𝑘−1+𝑄𝑘𝐵𝑘−2,𝐷𝐵𝑘−1=𝑃𝑘𝐺𝑘−1+𝑄𝑘𝐺𝑘−2.Gk−1=PkBk−1+QkBk−2,DBk−1=PkGk−1+QkGk−2.

    Therefore, multiplying the first equation by 𝐺𝑘−1Gk−1 and subtracting the second equation multiplied by 𝐵𝑘−1Bk−1, we have

    𝐺2𝑘−1−𝐷𝐵2𝑘−1=(𝐵𝑘−2𝐺𝑘−1−𝐵𝑘−1𝐺𝑘−2)𝑄𝑘=(𝐴𝑘−1𝐵𝑘−2−𝐵𝑘−1𝐴𝑘−2)𝑄0𝑄𝑘=(−1)𝑘𝑄0𝑄𝑘.Gk−12−DBk−12=(Bk−2Gk−1−Bk−1Gk−2)Qk=(Ak−1Bk−2−Bk−1Ak−2)Q0Qk=(−1)kQ0Qk.

    The last step uses the difference formula for convergents. This proves the first conclusion.

    To prove the second conclusion, substituting the expression for 𝐺𝑘Gk into the first conclusion gives

    (𝑄0𝐴𝑘−1−𝑃0𝐵𝑘−1)2−𝐷𝐵2𝑘−1=(−1)𝑘𝑄0𝑄𝑘.(Q0Ak−1−P0Bk−1)2−DBk−12=(−1)kQ0Qk.

    Therefore, using 𝑄0 ∣(𝑃20 −𝐷)Q0∣(P02−D),

    𝑄0𝐴2𝑘−1+(𝑃20−𝐷𝑄0𝐵𝑘−1−2𝑃0𝐴𝑘−1)𝐵𝑘−1=(−1)𝑘𝑄𝑘.Q0Ak−12+(P02−DQ0Bk−1−2P0Ak−1)Bk−1=(−1)kQk.

    Hence, gcd(𝐺𝑘−1,𝐵𝑘−1) =gcd(𝑄0𝐴𝑘−1,𝐵𝑘−1)gcd(Gk−1,Bk−1)=gcd(Q0Ak−1,Bk−1) divides 𝑄𝑘Qk.

    This conclusion provides a method to find solutions to the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N. If 𝑄0 >0Q0>0 is chosen reasonably and 𝑃0P0 is chosen as a solution to the congruence 𝑃20 ≡𝐷(mod𝑄0)P02≡D(modQ0), then by running the PQa algorithm on (𝑃0 +√𝐷)/𝑄0(P0+D)/Q0 until ( −1)𝑘𝑄0𝑄𝑘 =𝑁(−1)kQ0Qk=N is found, (𝐺𝑘−1,𝐵𝑘−1)(Gk−1,Bk−1) becomes a solution to the original equation. Moreover, if 𝑄𝑘 = ±1Qk=±1, then the solution obtained is necessarily primitive, meaning 𝐺𝑘−1Gk−1 and 𝐵𝑘−1Bk−1 are coprime.

    This idea is the core of solving Pell's equation and the generalized Pell equation. After understanding this idea, we now proceed to handle some details of the algorithm and prove that all solutions can be obtained through this method.

    Pell's Equation

    To solve the Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1, one only needs to run the PQa algorithm on (𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷) =(0,1,𝐷)(P0,Q0,D)=(0,1,D) until ( −1)𝑘𝑄𝑘 =1(−1)kQk=1 appears. At this point, (𝐴𝑘−1,𝐵𝑘−1)(Ak−1,Bk−1) is a solution to Pell's equation (since 𝐺𝑘−1Gk−1 is 𝐴𝑘−1Ak−1 at this time). Of course, for Pell's equation, this process can be described more precisely.

    First, solutions definitely appear at the end of the periodic part. This process is equivalent to performing the continued fraction expansion of √𝐷D. For this, there is already a conclusion:

    √𝐷=[⌊√𝐷⌋,―――――――――𝑎1,⋯,𝑎ℓ−1,2⌊√𝐷⌋].D=[⌊D⌋,a1,⋯,aℓ−1,2⌊D⌋―].

    Here, the period length is ℓℓ, and the starting position is the 1st term (index starts from 0). Moreover, its ℓℓ-th remainder equals ⌊√𝐷⌋ +√𝐷⌊D⌋+D, which shows 𝑄ℓ =1Qℓ=1. Therefore, if ℓℓ is even, then (𝐴ℓ−1,𝐵ℓ−1)(Aℓ−1,Bℓ−1) is a nontrivial solution of Pell's equation; if ℓℓ is odd, then (𝐴2ℓ−1,𝐵2ℓ−1)(A2ℓ−1,B2ℓ−1) is a nontrivial solution of Pell's equation.

    Next, we need to show that the solution obtained just now is definitely the fundamental solution. This conclusion is based on two reasons: first, all positive integer solutions (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) of Pell's equation correspond to fractions 𝑥/𝑦x/y that appear in the convergents of √𝐷D, which ensures that (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) must be some (𝐴𝑘,𝐵𝑘)(Ak,Bk) in the PQa algorithm process; second, except for the end of the periodic part, no other position has 𝑄𝑘 =1Qk=1, because the recurrence relation of 𝐴𝑘Ak and 𝐵𝑘Bk guarantees their values increase with the index, so the smallest positive integer solution (i.e., the fundamental solution) must appear at the position just indicated. These two reasons can be derived from the following two theorems respectively:

    Theorem

    Suppose the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N has a positive integer solution (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y). If |𝑁| <√𝐷|N|<D, then 𝑥𝑦xy must equal a convergent of √𝐷D.

    Proof

    When 𝑁 >0N>0, since 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 >0x2−Dy2>0, we have 𝑥 >𝑦√𝐷x>yD. Hence,

    ∣𝑥𝑦−√𝐷∣=𝑁𝑦(𝑥+𝑦√𝐷)<𝑁2𝑦2√𝐷<12𝑦2.|xy−D|=Ny(x+yD)<N2y2D<12y2.

    According to Legendre's Criterion, 𝑥𝑦xy is a convergent of √𝐷D.

    When 𝑁 <0N<0, 𝑥 >𝑦√𝐷x>yD no longer holds. So we instead consider the solutions of 𝑦2 −1𝐷𝑥2 = −𝑁𝐷y2−1Dx2=−ND. Since |𝑁|𝐷 <√1𝐷|N|D<1D, the above argument still holds. This shows 𝑦𝑥yx is a convergent of 1√𝐷1D. According to the Reciprocal Theorem, 𝑥𝑦xy is also a convergent of √𝐷D.

    Theorem

    In the process of running the above PQa algorithm on (𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷) =(0,1,𝐷)(P0,Q0,D)=(0,1,D), 𝑄𝑘 =1Qk=1 necessarily implies ℓ ∣𝑘ℓ∣k.

    Proof

    In the continued fraction expansion of √𝐷D, except for the 0-th remainder, all other remainders are purely periodic continued fractions. Suppose 𝑄𝑘 =1Qk=1. According to Galois's result, there must be a remainder 𝜔𝑘 =𝑃𝑘 +√𝐷 >1ωk=Pk+D>1, and its conjugate −1 <𝑃𝑘 −√𝐷 <0−1<Pk−D<0, which means 𝑃𝑘 =⌊√𝐷⌋Pk=⌊D⌋. Therefore, the remainder 𝜔𝑘ωk equals 𝜔ℓωℓ. However, repetition of remainders implies periodicity of the continued fraction. If 𝑘k is not a multiple of ℓℓ, it contradicts that ℓℓ is the minimal positive period. So necessarily ℓ ∣𝑘ℓ∣k.

    Synthesizing the discussion in this section, as long as we perform the continued fraction expansion of √𝐷D, i.e., start the PQa algorithm with (𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷) =(0,1,𝐷)(P0,Q0,D)=(0,1,D), when we first obtain 𝑄ℓ =1Qℓ=1, we have reached the end of the first period. At this point, if ℓℓ is even, then (𝐴ℓ−1,𝐵ℓ−1)(Aℓ−1,Bℓ−1) is the fundamental solution of Pell's equation; otherwise, (𝐴2ℓ−1,𝐵2ℓ−1)(A2ℓ−1,B2ℓ−1) is the fundamental solution of Pell's equation. For the case where the period length ℓℓ is odd, one does not need to continue the PQa algorithm to twice the period length; it will be explained immediately that 𝐴2ℓ−1 +𝐵2ℓ−1√𝐷 =(𝐴ℓ−1 +𝐵ℓ−1√𝐷)2A2ℓ−1+B2ℓ−1D=(Aℓ−1+Bℓ−1D)2, so the fundamental solution of Pell's equation can be directly calculated from (𝐴ℓ−1,𝐵ℓ−1)(Aℓ−1,Bℓ−1). All other solutions of Pell's equation can be computed from the fundamental solution.

    Example

    1. Solve the equation 𝑥2 −14𝑦2 =1x2−14y2=1.

      Running the PQa algorithm on (𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷) =(0,1,14)(P0,Q0,D)=(0,1,14) gives the following results: (the red part is the first period)

    2. Solve the equation 𝑥2 −41𝑦2 =1x2−41y2=1.

    Negative Pell Equation

    According to the discussion in the previous section, solutions to the negative Pell equation must also correspond to convergents of √𝐷D, and can only appear at positions where ( −1)𝑘𝑄𝑘 = −1(−1)kQk=−1. This can only occur at the end of the periodic part. Therefore, the negative Pell equation has solutions if and only if the period length ℓℓ is odd. When a solution exists, (𝐴ℓ−1,𝐵ℓ−1)(Aℓ−1,Bℓ−1) is the fundamental solution of the negative Pell equation. Its solution method is the same as in the previous section.

    Using a proof similar to that for the structure of solutions to Pell's equation, the following conclusion can be proved:

    Theorem

    Suppose the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −1x2−Dy2=−1 has a solution, and its fundamental solution is (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1). Then all integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1 belong to the set

    {(𝑥,𝑦):𝑥+𝑦√𝐷=±(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷)𝑘,𝑘∈𝐙}.{(x,y):x+yD=±(x1+y1D)k,k∈Z}.

    In particular, the integer solution (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) satisfying 𝑥2 +𝑦2√𝐷 =(𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷)2x2+y2D=(x1+y1D)2 is exactly the fundamental solution of 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1.

    Proof

    Due to symmetry, we only need to consider positive integer solutions, i.e., 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷 >1x+yD>1. However, since 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1 consists of two branches of the hyperbola, 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD cannot establish a one-to-one correspondence with (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y). To handle this difficulty, first prove that the above (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) is the fundamental solution of 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1.

    Obviously, (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) is a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1. If (𝑧,𝑤)(z,w) is the fundamental solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1, then we must have 1 <𝑧 +𝑤√𝐷 ≤𝑥2 +𝑦2√𝐷1<z+wD≤x2+y2D. If the right inequality does not include equality, then dividing the inequality by 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D gives −𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷 <(𝑧 +𝑤√𝐷)( −𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷) <𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷−x1+y1D<(z+wD)(−x1+y1D)<x1+y1D. Expanding the middle term of this inequality yields the form 𝑥′ +𝑦′√𝐷x′+y′D, whose norm is −1−1 and (𝑥′,𝑦′)(x′,y′) is also an integer solution. Taking the reciprocal of this inequality shows that −𝑥′ +𝑦′√𝐷−x′+y′D also lies between −𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷−x1+y1D and 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D. The quadratic integers ±𝑥′ +𝑦′√𝐷±x′+y′D are reciprocals of each other, and one must be greater than 11. However, there should be no other quadratic integers with norm −1−1 between 11 and 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D, which contradicts the minimality of 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D. Therefore, we must have 𝑥2 +𝑦2√𝐷 =𝑧 +𝑤√𝐷x2+y2D=z+wD, i.e., (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) is the fundamental solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1.

    Based on this, if there is a solution (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1 that does not correspond to some (𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷)𝑘(x1+y1D)k, then there must exist a 𝑘k such that (𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷)2𝑘 <𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷 <(𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷)2𝑘+2(x1+y1D)2k<x+yD<(x1+y1D)2k+2. Factoring out (𝑥1 +𝑦1)2𝑘+1(x1+y1)2k+1, it shows there exists a quadratic integer 𝑥′ +𝑦′√𝐷 ≠1x′+y′D≠1 with norm ±1±1 lying between −𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷−x1+y1D and 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D. Repeating the argument using reciprocals from the previous paragraph shows this contradicts the minimality of 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D. Thus the original proposition is proven.

    Since (𝐴ℓ−1,𝐵ℓ−1)(Aℓ−1,Bℓ−1) is the minimal positive integer solution of the negative Pell equation, and all positive integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1 appear in the set

    {(𝑥,𝑦):𝑥+𝑦√𝐷=(𝐴ℓ−1+𝐵ℓ−1√𝐷)𝑘,𝑘∈𝐍+}{(x,y):x+yD=(Aℓ−1+Bℓ−1D)k,k∈N+}

    and since these positive integer solutions must correspond to convergents at the end of the periodic part of √𝐷D (the previous position), and the numerators and denominators of convergents are strictly increasing, we always have

    (𝐴ℓ−1+𝐵ℓ−1√𝐷)𝑘=𝐴𝑘ℓ−1+𝐵𝑘ℓ−1√𝐷.(Aℓ−1+Bℓ−1D)k=Akℓ−1+Bkℓ−1D.

    Among all these positive integer solutions, when 𝑘k is odd they are solutions to the negative Pell equation, and when 𝑘k is even they are solutions to Pell's equation, alternating.

    To determine whether the negative Pell equation has solutions, one needs to calculate the period length of the continued fraction expansion of √𝐷D, which is not easy to compute. Therefore, we hope to find a simpler judgment method. However, there is currently no condition that is simple and easy to compute[^solubility-neg-pell]. We only provide a simple conclusion here.

    Theorem

    The equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −1x2−Dy2=−1 has solutions only if 44 does not divide 𝐷D and 𝐷D does not contain prime factors of the form 4𝑘 +34k+3. Conversely, if 𝐷 =2D=2 or 𝐷D is a prime of the form 4𝑘 +14k+1, then the equation certainly has solutions.

    Proof

    First, if the negative Pell equation has solutions, then −1−1 is a quadratic residue modulo 𝐷D, hence −1−1 is also a quadratic residue modulo any divisor 𝑑d of 𝐷D, so 𝑑 ≠4d≠4 and 𝑑d is not a prime of the form 4𝑘 +34k+3. Conversely, the equation 𝑥2 −2𝑦2 = −1x2−2y2=−1 has a nontrivial solution (1,1)(1,1). The remaining case is when 𝐷D is a prime of the form 4𝑘 +14k+1.

    Let 𝐷D be a prime of the form 4𝑘 +14k+1. The idea is to start with the fundamental solution (𝑢,𝑣)(u,v) of the Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1 and construct a solution (𝛼,𝛽)(α,β) to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −1x2−Dy2=−1. If 𝑢u is even, reducing 𝑢2 −𝐷𝑣2 =1u2−Dv2=1 modulo 44 gives 𝑣2 ≡ −1(mod4)v2≡−1(mod4), but −1−1 is not a quadratic residue modulo 44. This contradiction shows 𝑢u is odd. Consider the equation 𝐷𝑣2 =𝑢2 −1 =(𝑢 +1)(𝑢 −1)Dv2=u2−1=(u+1)(u−1). Since 𝑢u is odd, gcd(𝑢 +1,𝑢 −1) =gcd(𝑢 +1,2) =2gcd(u+1,u−1)=gcd(u+1,2)=2. Based on this fact, the factors of 𝐷𝑣2Dv2 are distributed to 𝑢 +1u+1 and 𝑢 −1u−1, one must be 2𝛼22α2 and the other 2𝐷𝛽22Dβ2, where 𝛼α and 𝛽β are coprime positive integers and 𝑣 =2𝛼𝛽v=2αβ. Substituting 𝑢 =𝛼2 +𝐷𝛽2u=α2+Dβ2 and 𝑣 =2𝛼𝛽v=2αβ into 𝑢2 −𝐷𝑣2 =1u2−Dv2=1 yields 𝛼2 −𝐷𝛽2 = ±1α2−Dβ2=±1. Since (𝑢,𝑣)(u,v) is the fundamental solution to Pell's equation and (𝛼,𝛽)(α,β) is a smaller positive integer pair than (𝑢,𝑣)(u,v), the right side cannot be +1+1, so it must be −1−1. This proves that 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −1x2−Dy2=−1 has a solution (𝛼,𝛽)(α,β).

    If 𝐷D is composite, then being square-free and not containing prime factors of the form 4𝑘 +34k+3 does not guarantee that 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −1x2−Dy2=−1 has solutions—for example, 𝑥2 −34𝑦2 = −1x2−34y2=−1 has no solutions.

    Example

    Using the calculation results from the examples above, the equation 𝑥2 −14𝑦2 = −1x2−14y2=−1 has no solutions, and the minimal positive integer solution of 𝑥2 −41𝑦2 = −1x2−41y2=−1 is (𝐺2,𝐵2) =(32,5)(G2,B2)=(32,5).

    The Case of Norm ±4

    Next, we discuss solutions to the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4. At this time, the behavior of solutions depends on the value of 𝐷mod4Dmod4.

    Some cases are easy. If 𝐷 ≡0(mod4)D≡0(mod4), then 𝑥x is even, so (𝑥/2,𝑦)(x/2,y) is a solution to 𝑢2 −(𝐷/4)𝑣2 = ±1u2−(D/4)v2=±1. In the remaining cases, 𝑥x and 𝑦y must be both odd or both even. If 𝑥x and 𝑦y are both odd, reducing both sides modulo 44 yields 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4). So if 𝐷 ≡2,3(mod4)D≡2,3(mod4), then 𝑥x and 𝑦y can only be both even, so (𝑥/2,𝑦/2)(x/2,y/2) is a solution to 𝑢2 −𝐷𝑣2 = ±1u2−Dv2=±1.     Let 𝐷D be a positive integer that is not a perfect square. The continued fraction expansion of the quadratic irrational 𝜔 =1+√𝐷2ω=1+D2 has the form

    Theorem

    Let the minimal positive integer solution of the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4 be (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1). Then all its solutions are

    ⎧{ {⎨{ {⎩(𝑥,𝑦):𝑥+𝑦√𝐷2=±(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷2)𝑘,𝑘∈𝐙⎫{ {⎬{ {⎭.{(x,y):x+yD2=±(x1+y1D2)k,k∈Z}.
    Proof

    Due to symmetry, we only need to consider positive integer solutions (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y). What needs to be proved here is only that the real pairs (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) in the set are indeed integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4. The remaining part only needs to restate the proof of the structure of solutions to the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1.

    Actually, what needs to be proved is that for any integer solutions (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) and (𝑥2,𝑦2)(x2,y2) to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4, the following defined positive real pair (𝑥3,𝑦3)(x3,y3) is still an integer solution:

    Expanding the right-hand side and comparing coefficients of rational and irrational terms gives

    𝑥3=𝑥1𝑥2+𝐷𝑦1𝑦22, 𝑦3=𝑥1𝑦2+𝑥2𝑦12.x3=x1x2+Dy1y22, y3=x1y2+x2y12.

    Since for 𝑖 =1,2i=1,2 we have 𝑥𝑖 ≡𝑥2𝑖 ≡𝐷𝑦2𝑖 ≡𝐷𝑦𝑖(mod2)xi≡xi2≡Dyi2≡Dyi(mod2), we have

    2𝑥3=𝑥1𝑥2+𝐷𝑦1𝑦2≡𝐷2𝑦1𝑦2+𝐷𝑦1𝑦2=𝐷(𝐷+1)𝑦1𝑦2≡0(mod2),2𝑦3=𝑥1𝑦2+𝑥2𝑦1≡𝐷𝑦1𝑦2+𝐷𝑦2𝑦1=2𝐷𝑦1𝑦2≡0(mod2).2x3=x1x2+Dy1y2≡D2y1y2+Dy1y2=D(D+1)y1y2≡0(mod2),2y3=x1y2+x2y1≡Dy1y2+Dy2y1=2Dy1y2≡0(mod2).

    This shows 𝑥3x3 and 𝑦3y3 are both integers. Then using the property that norm is multiplicative, (𝑥3,𝑦3)(x3,y3) is a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4.

    Synthesizing these facts and repeating the discussions from the previous sections, we can explain the correctness of the algorithm for solving 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4. These results show that the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4 has a simple solution structure similar to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1: all its solutions can be expressed through its minimal positive integer solution without solving other equations.

    In fact, all solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1 can be found among solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4, so from this perspective, 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4 is more fundamental. Obviously, (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) is a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1 if and only if (2𝑥,2𝑦)(2x,2y) is a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4. The analysis above indicates that when 𝐷 ≡2,3(mod4)D≡2,3(mod4), all solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4 are necessarily both even, so they correspond to solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1.

    When 𝐷 ≡0(mod4)D≡0(mod4), among solutions (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4, 𝑥x must be even, but 𝑦y may be odd. If in the minimal positive integer solution (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4, 𝑦1y1 is even, then 𝑦y is even in all solutions, so these integer solutions correspond one-to-one with integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1; however, if in the minimal integer solution (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1), 𝑦1y1 is odd, then the parity of 𝑦𝑘yk will be consistent with 𝑘k, alternating, so only when 𝑘k is even does it correspond to a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1. If in the minimal positive integer solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4, 𝑦1y1 is odd and the norm of 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D is −4−4, then for such 𝐷D, 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −4x2−Dy2=−4 has solutions, but 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −1x2−Dy2=−1 has no solutions.

    When 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4), solutions (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4 may be both odd or both even. If the minimal positive integer solution (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) is already both even, then all its integer solutions are also both even, so they always correspond to integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1. If the minimal positive integer solution (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1) is both odd, we have the following conclusion:

    Theorem

    Let the minimal positive integer solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4 be (𝑥1,𝑦1)(x1,y1). If 𝑥1x1 and 𝑦1y1 are both odd, then 𝐷 ≡5(mod8)D≡5(mod8), and the integer solution (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) is even if and only if

    𝑥+𝑦√𝐷2=±(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷2)3𝑘,𝑘∈𝐙.x+yD2=±(x1+y1D2)3k,k∈Z.
    Proof

    Reducing both sides of 𝑥21 −𝐷𝑦21 = ±4x12−Dy12=±4 modulo 88 gives 𝐷 ≡5(mod8)D≡5(mod8). To prove the second conclusion, first prove that (𝑥3,𝑦3)(x3,y3) are both even, because

    𝑥3+𝑦3√𝐷2=(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷2)3=𝑥31+3𝐷𝑥𝑦218+3𝑥21𝑦1+𝐷𝑦318√𝐷,x3+y3D2=(x1+y1D2)3=x13+3Dxy128+3x12y1+Dy138D,

    so we only need to prove the right-hand side is an integer. Since the square of an odd number is 11 modulo 88, we have

    𝑥31+3𝐷𝑥𝑦1=𝑥1(𝑥21+3𝐷𝑦1)≡𝑥1(1+3×5×1)=16𝑥1=0(mod8),3𝑥21𝑦1+𝐷𝑦31=𝑦1(3𝑥21+𝐷𝑦21)≡𝑦1(3×1+5×1)=8𝑦1=0(mod8).x13+3Dxy1=x1(x12+3Dy1)≡x1(1+3×5×1)=16x1=0(mod8),3x12y1+Dy13=y1(3x12+Dy12)≡y1(3×1+5×1)=8y1=0(mod8).

    This shows 𝑥3,𝑦3x3,y3 are both even. Then for all 𝑘 ∈𝐙k∈Z, we have

    𝑥+𝑦√𝐷2=±(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷2)3𝑘=±(𝑥3+𝑦3√𝐷2)𝑘∈𝐙,x+yD2=±(x1+y1D2)3k=±(x3+y3D2)k∈Z,

    so at this time (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) are both even. Conversely, for 𝑟 =1,2r=1,2, we always have

    ±(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷2)3𝑘+𝑟=±(𝑥3+𝑦3√𝐷2)𝑘(𝑥𝑟+𝑦𝑟√𝐷2).±(x1+y1D2)3k+r=±(x3+y3D2)k(xr+yrD2).

    To prove the corresponding (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) are not integers, we only need to prove the right-hand side is not an integer. For 𝑟 =1r=1, this is the known condition; for 𝑟 =2r=2, because

    𝑥2+𝑦2√𝐷2=(𝑥1+𝑦1√𝐷2)2=𝑥21+𝐷𝑦214+𝑥1𝑦12√𝐷,x2+y2D2=(x1+y1D2)2=x12+Dy124+x1y12D,

    and 𝑥21 +𝐷𝑦21 ≡1 +1 ×1 =2(mod4)x12+Dy12≡1+1×1=2(mod4), 𝑥1𝑦1 ≡1(mod2)x1y1≡1(mod2), so this expression is also not an integer. This proves that only when the exponent is a multiple of 33 are the corresponding solutions all even.

    That is, among every three solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4, one is both even, which corresponds to integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1. This also shows that for 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4), 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −4x2−Dy2=−4 has solutions if and only if 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −1x2−Dy2=−1 has solutions.

    The discussion so far is sufficient to compute the fundamental units of the real quadratic integer ring. Let 𝐷D be a positive integer without square factors. For 𝐷 ≡2,3(mod4)D≡2,3(mod4), one only needs to find the minimal positive integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1; for 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4), one only needs to find the minimal positive integer solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4. When the minimal positive integer solution (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) is obtained, for 𝐷 ≡2,3(mod4)D≡2,3(mod4), the fundamental unit is ±𝑥 ±𝑦√𝐷±x±yD; for 𝐷 ≡1(mod4)D≡1(mod4), the fundamental unit is ±𝑥±𝑦√𝐷2±x±yD2.

    General Case

    Finally, we discuss the solution method for the generalized Pell equation.

    For the case |𝑁| <√𝐷|N|<D, there is a simple solution method. The conclusion from earlier shows that solutions (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) to the equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N must satisfy 𝑥𝑦xy equals some convergent of √𝐷D. Moreover, according to the solution structure discussed earlier, each fundamental solution (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) satisfies 𝑥 +𝑦√𝐷x+yD being less than or equal to the fundamental solution 𝑥1 +𝑦1√𝐷x1+y1D of the corresponding Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =1x2−Dy2=1. Using the monotonicity of the denominator sequence 𝐵𝑘Bk in the PQa algorithm, these fundamental solutions to the generalized Pell equation must appear before the fundamental solution of the corresponding Pell equation. Therefore, one only needs to run the PQa algorithm on (𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷) =(0,1,𝐷)(P0,Q0,D)=(0,1,D) until 𝑄ℓ′ =1Qℓ′=1 and ℓ′ℓ′ is even. During this process, for each (𝐴𝑘,𝐵𝑘)(Ak,Bk) that appears, check whether there exists an integer 𝑓f such that

holds. If it does, then $(fA_k, fB_k)$ is recorded as a minimal positive integer solution. All $(fA_k, fB_k)$ recorded in this process are the complete minimal positive integer solutions to the equation $x^2-Dy^2=N$. Using $(A_{\ell'-1},B_{\ell'-1})$, i.e., the fundamental solution of the corresponding Pell equation, all solutions to the generalized Pell equation can be generated from these minimal positive integer solutions. Note that depending on whether the period length $\ell$ is even or odd, $\ell'$ may be $\ell$ or $2\ell$.

    For the more general case of 𝑁N, the above method no longer applies. First, enumerate all square factors 𝑓2f2 of 𝑁N, let 𝑚 =𝑁/𝑓2m=N/f2, and enumerate all solutions 𝑧z to the congruence 𝑧2 ≡𝐷(mod|𝑚|)z2≡D(mod|m|) satisfying −|𝑚|/2 <𝑧 ≤|𝑚|/2−|m|/2<z≤|m|/2. Then run the PQa algorithm on (𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷) =(𝑧,|𝑚|,𝐷)(P0,Q0,D)=(z,|m|,D) until 𝑄𝑘 = ±1Qk=±1 or a period has already completed. In the second case, there is no solution to the equation related to this set (𝑓,𝑧)(f,z). In the first case, further determine whether ( −1)𝑘𝑄𝑘 =𝑁/|𝑁|(−1)kQk=N/|N| matches. If they match in sign, then (𝑓𝐺𝑘−1,𝑓𝐵𝑘−1)(fGk−1,fBk−1) is a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N; otherwise, it is a solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = −𝑁x2−Dy2=−N, and only when the corresponding negative Pell equation has solutions can the solution to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N be obtained by combining it with the fundamental solution of the corresponding negative Pell equation. After completing the traversal of all sets (𝑓,𝑧)(f,z), we obtain exactly one solution in each equivalence class of solutions to 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 =𝑁x2−Dy2=N, and that solution is the fundamental solution or minimal positive integer solution in that equivalence class. Using them together with the fundamental solution of the corresponding Pell equation, all integer solutions to the equation can be generated. This algorithm is called the Lagrange–Matthews–Mollin algorithm.

    The correctness of this algorithm is guaranteed by the following theorem:

    This theorem guarantees that all positive solutions to the equation exist in the convergents of the corresponding quadratic irrational. Because when using the PQa algorithm to compute convergents, once entering the periodic part, it can be guaranteed that the convergents are always positive. Therefore, as long as we enumerate all quadratic irrationals allowed by the theorem conditions and compute their convergents until within one period, we can find a solution. Since two solutions appearing in the convergents of the same quadratic irrational are definitely equivalent, we only need to get the first solution satisfying ( −1)𝑘𝑄𝑘 =𝑁/|𝑁|(−1)kQk=N/|N| and stop the subsequent calculations. Different from all previous algorithms, here the 𝑘k satisfying the condition may appear before entering the period.
